profile.name: Canadian stepdance
profile.tagline: Lively percussive footwork born from European traditions in Canadian logging camps.
profile.insight: Brought to Nova Scotia by 18th-century Scottish Gaels, Cape Breton stepdance died out in its Highland homeland but survived in Canada, where it was later re-introduced back to Scotland.
profile.profile: Canadian stepdance encompasses several regional percussive folk dance styles brought to Canada by French, Irish, and Scottish settlers. Dancers execute sharp heel taps, toe taps, and shuffles while keeping within a compact footprint. Regional variants include Cape Breton, Quebecois, Ottawa Valley, Newfoundland, and Métis styles. The dance is performed to live fiddle tunes including fast reels in 4/4 time, energetic jigs in 6/8, and slower clogs.
profile.profile_long:
Canadian stepdance refers to several related forms of percussive stepdance in Canada with European origins including France, Ireland, and Scotland. Canadian stepdancing involves percussive dancing to Celtic tunes, usually played by a fiddle. Percussive sounds are created through a combination of foot movements such as heel taps, toe taps, and shuffles, all designed to accentuate the music. Canadian stepdance is normally danced in a small space with limited lateral movement. Upper-body postures in Canadian stepdancing are typically relaxed but upright, allowing occasional arm movements that flow with the rhythm of the dance, or hands resting on hips.

Stepdance steps vary according to the Celtic tune type played, such as jigs, reels, strathspeys, clogs, hornpipes, two-steps, and polkas. A reel, the most common tune type in Canadian stepdance, is played in 4/4 time, and is fun, fast, and lively. A jig, also quite popular, is played in 6/8 time and sounds like an energetic march. The clog is slower, danced in half time, and is considered to be a more graceful dance.

There are numerous Canadian stepdance styles found in different regions of Canada. Cape Breton stepdance is unique to the Cape Breton Island region of Nova Scotia, brought there by large numbers of Scottish Gaelic settlers who arrived in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. The style originated in the Scottish Highlands and Western Islands, emerging from solo step dances that were likely not originally percussive in nature. While this style was preserved in Cape Breton through informal generational transmission in homes, the tradition died out in Scotland before being re-introduced.

French Canadian or Quebecois stepdance originates from the lumber camps and villages of Quebec, taking influence from Irish and Breton dance. Ottawa Valley stepdance, found in the Ottawa Valley, features variable, aggressive steps danced high off the floor, alongside flowing arm movements and incorporated tap dance elements. Ottawa Valley style also originated in lumber camps as leisure after hard physical work. Other prominent regional variants include Newfoundland stepdance and Métis stepdance style, known as jigging.

sections.origins_and_history: Canadian stepdance has European origins including France, Ireland, and Scotland. Large numbers of Scottish Gaelic settlers arrived on Cape Breton Island in Nova Scotia during the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, bringing stepdance traditions from the Scottish Highlands and Western Islands. While the tradition died out in Scotland, it was preserved in Canada and eventually re-introduced to its homeland. Other styles developed in Quebec and the Ottawa Valley, originating in lumber camps and villages as a form of leisure after hard work.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Canadian stepdance is normally danced in a small space with limited lateral movement. Percussive sounds are created through a combination of foot movements such as heel taps, toe taps, and shuffles designed to accentuate the music. Upper-body postures are typically relaxed but upright, allowing occasional arm movements that flow with the rhythm or hands on hips. Steps vary according to the tune: reels in 4/4 time are fast and lively, jigs in 6/8 time sound like energetic marches, and clogs are slower and half-time. Ottawa Valley style features variable, aggressive steps danced high off the floor.
sections.music_and_instruments: Canadian stepdancing involves percussive dancing to Celtic tunes, usually played by a fiddle. The steps strictly mirror tune types including reels, jigs, strathspeys, clogs, hornpipes, two-steps, and polkas. A reel is played in 4/4 time, while a jig is played in 6/8 time. The clog is played and danced in a slower half-time tempo.
sections.costume_and_setting: Canadian stepdance is performed in small spaces with limited lateral movement. Historically, regional styles like French Canadian and Ottawa Valley stepdance were performed in lumber camps and village settings.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Stepdancing served as informal domestic recreation and social leisure after hard work in lumber camps and rural villages. Transmission was traditionally generational within the home among family and neighbours, though formal classes emerged around the 1970s.
sections.regional_variants: Regional styles include Cape Breton stepdance in Nova Scotia, French Canadian or Quebecois stepdance taking influence from Irish and Breton dance, Ottawa Valley stepdance featuring tap elements and high aggressive steps, Newfoundland stepdance, and Métis stepdance style known as jigging.
sections.lineage: Evolved from 18th-century Scottish Highland solo step dances, Irish step dance, Breton dance, and French traditional folk dances, with Ottawa Valley style incorporating elements of American tap dance.
